analysis.one_liner: Repeals campaign finance rules restricting corporate and union election ads.
analysis.headline: A bill to roll back parts of the 2002 campaign finance law never got a hearing or vote; it died in committee at the end of the 110th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would erase the portion of the 2002 Bipartisan Campaign Reform Act (the 'McCain-Feingold' law) that governs 'electioneering communications' — TV and radio ads that name a federal candidate shortly before an election. It would repeal both the requirement to disclose who paid for those ads and the special rule that lets corporations, unions, and banks fund them through segregated 'connected' accounts paid by members. After repeal, those groups could spend corporate or union treasury money on candidate-focused ads with no disclosure. The bill was referred to the House Administration Committee and never received a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Corporations (including national banks), labor unions, and wealthy interests that spend on election advertising. Repealing disclosure would let big spenders influence close elections anonymously; repealing the funding rules would let groups use general treasury money rather than a segregated account of voluntary contributions. Very wealthy donors and groups running 'issue ads' close to elections would gain the most — they could air ads attacking or supporting candidates without any public paper trail.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Corporate ad spenders, unions, wealthy donors

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the requirement to report who paid for broadcast ads that name a federal candidate within 30 days of a primary or 60 days of a general election, allowing anonymous political spending.

Removes the framework under which corporations, unions, and banks could fund election ads only through segregated accounts of voluntary contributions, opening the door to treasury-funded electioneering.

analysis.who_pays: Voters and small donors: they would no longer be able to see who was paying for last-minute political ads, making it harder to judge the source and motive of campaign messages. Ordinary citizens' influence relative to large corporate or union treasuries would shrink.
analysis.who_pays_short: Voters' access to ad sponsorship information

drawbacks.text: Eliminates disclosure, so voters could no longer find out which corporation, union, or bank paid for ads hitting a candidate days before an election.

Supporters argued the rules burden First Amendment rights; critics viewed repeal as enabling large, unaccountable spending to dominate elections. The bill also repealed rules limiting electioneering funded by foreign nationals' involvement in some channels.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit claimed was deregulating political speech to protect First Amendment activity. The cost was near-total loss of transparency for big-money ads close to elections, shifting influence toward those with the largest treasuries. Weighing these, the bill primarily served large institutional spenders rather than ordinary voters.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced and referred to the House Administration Committee in October 2007, it never received a hearing or vote before the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on October 1, 2007 and referred the same day to the House Committee on House Administration, which was its final recorded action.
No further action, markup, or vote occurred before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent members of Congress and major corporate, union, and banking interests that benefit from the existing campaign finance framework were spared the disruption of repeal; voters saw no change to disclosure rules. Because the bill died quietly, the status quo prevailed and no interest group gained or lost materially from this specific bill's fate.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Incumbents and existing big-money ad spenders

for.name: Mike Pence
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the McCain-Feingold electioneering-communications provisions.

against.name: House Committee on House Administration
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and took no further action, so the bill never came to a vote.

sides.party_line_note: Only a sponsor and two Republican cosponsors are on record; no committee or floor votes show where the broader House stood.

industries.note: Repeal would expand the pool of money spent on last-minute political ads, increasing demand for broadcast airtime, but with no disclosure requirement. Voters lose the ability to identify who is funding the messages they see.
